papers.title: Temporal evolution of EEG hallmarks in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
papers.title_zh: 儿童期Lennox-Gastaut综合征脑电图标志的时间演变
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: The temporal development of generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) and slow spike-and-wave complexes in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) remains poorly characterized. This study mapped the emergence and longitudinal evolution of these EEG hallmarks in a real-world LGS cohort.
METHODS: This retrospective observational cohort study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric neurophysiology and neurology center. Patients aged 1-18 years fulfilling current International League Against Epilepsy criteria for LGS were identified through local databases. All available sleep video-EEG recordings before November 2024 were reviewed; clinical features, EEG findings, and comorbidities were collected at each recording. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: We reviewed 234 EEGs from 51 patients (75% male). Median age at first EEG was 5 years. GPFA emerged later than slow spike-and-wave (mean age: 9.6 vs 8.3 years, p = 0.002), with non-parametric analysis confirming a significant difference in age at first detection (p = 0.004). Median age at epilepsy onset was 1.1 years, while all clinical and EEG criteria for LGS were met at a median age of 10.9 years.
CONCLUSION: EEG hallmarks of LGS emerged progressively during childhood, with slow spike-and-wave preceding GPFA during sleep. Following early clinical manifestations, a prolonged developmental phase may precede full electroclinical expression of LGS, with implications for early diagnosis and longitudinal EEG surveillance.

papers.title: Absence of familial adult myoclonic epilepsy-associated intronic repeat expansions in SAMD12, STARD7, and MARCHF6 genes in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy with tremor.
papers.title_zh: 在青少年肌阵挛性癫痫伴震颤的SAMD12、STARD7和MARCHF6基因中无家族性成人肌阵挛性癫痫相关内含子重复扩增。
papers.abstract: We investigated whether intronic repeat expansions in the SAMD12, STARD7, and MARCHF6 genes are present in individuals with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) and tremor. Given that tremor is a shared feature with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME), we hypothesized that this phenotype may reflect a common genetic basis involving FAME-associated pentanucleotide repeat expansions. The study included 31 individuals with JME and tremor (17/31 [54.8%] females, mean age at genetic testing = 34.4 ± 13.8 years) and 100 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Genomic DNA was analyzed using repeat-primed polymerase chain reaction and fragment analysis to detect intronic TTTCA repeat expansions in the three established FAME-associated genes. No pathogenic repeat expansions were identified in SAMD12, STARD7, or MARCHF6 among individuals with JME and tremor. The frequency of intronic pentanucleotide repeat expansions did not differ between cases and controls. This is a comprehensive analysis assessing three FAME-associated repeat-expansion loci in a clinically well-characterized cohort of individuals with JME and tremor. Our findings do not support a major contribution of these FAME-associated loci to tremor in this cohort, suggesting that those intronic repeats did not contribute to genetic susceptibility to the tremor in JME. Further studies are required to identify the factors associated with this phenotype.

papers.title: Transition of spike to seizure networks in the rat somatosensory and motor cortex requires mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling.
papers.title_zh: 大鼠躯体感觉和运动皮层中的刺突向癫痫发作网络的转变需要有丝分裂原激活蛋白激酶信号传导。
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: During epileptogenesis, epileptic spikes emerge before seizures, yet the network mechanisms linking spike activity to seizure generation remain unclear. Previously, we showed that mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MAP2K) inhibition reduces spiking in tetanus toxin (TeNT)-injected rats. Here, we advanced the TeNT rat model to transition from spike to seizure networks to better understand the mechanisms underlying this process and determined the effect of MAP2K inhibition on both spikes and seizures.
METHODS: Male rats received a single injection of TeNT into the somatosensory cortex (SC) or motor cortex (MC). Long-term video-electroencephalographic recordings over bilateral SC and MC were obtained for up to 140 days and analyzed using automated algorithms to quantify spike frequency, propagation, synchrony, and electrographic seizures. A subset of animals was treated orally with the MAP2K inhibitor CI-1040 (250 mg/kg/day) on Days 14-35 to assess its effects on spike and seizure network formation.
RESULTS: Low-dose TeNT (60-120 ng/μL) injection into the SC produced progressive bihemispheric spiking without seizure development. In contrast, high-dose TeNT (250 ng/μL) injection into the SC, but not MC, induced spontaneous electrographic seizures in five of eight animals. Before the first detected seizure, spikes were observed in both the ipsilateral and contralateral hemispheres. However, only animals whose propagation pattern became more synchronous developed seizures. Spike frequency did not differ between SC- and MC-injected animals. Early inhibition of MAP2K using CI-1040 reduced spike frequency and spike synchrony and was associated with an absence of detected seizures.
SIGNIFICANCE: These findings demonstrate that the transition from interictal spikes to seizures in the rat sensory-motor system involves bihemispheric spike networks that transition into seizure networks. We show that SC is more prone to seizure development than MC and suggest that MAPK signaling contributes to bihemispheric spike synchronization, which could be important for seizure development.

papers.title: Stability of the Epileptogenic Index across seizures and the effects of sleep and withdrawal of anti-seizure medications.
papers.title_zh: 癫痫发作中癫痫发作指数的稳定性以及睡眠和停用抗癫痫药物的影响。
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Epileptogenic Index (EI) is a promising index to evaluate the epileptogenicity of the brain tissue and is useful in planning epilepsy surgery. We aimed to evaluate whether EI maps are consistent across seizures within patients and whether EI-derived measures are affected by the vigilance state and anti-seizure medication (ASM) dose.
METHODS: We analyzed 127 stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) seizures from 19 patients. EI was calculated in all seizures. Within-patient EI consistency was assessed using pairwise Spearman correlations between seizure-specific EI maps. To assess the effects of vigilance and ASM on EI consistency, we calculated a contact-level p_weighted EI score that combines the frequency of suprathreshold EI involvement and mean EI magnitude, separately across vigilance states and in a subset of patients with different ASM states.
RESULTS: Mean seizure-to-seizure EI correlations ranged from 0.11 to 0.81, indicating substantial variability in within-patient EI consistency. Seven patients showed high consistency (≥0.6) and four showed low consistency (≤0.3). At the contact level, no differences in p_weighted EI were found between wakefulness and sleep. In contrast, p_weighted EI was significantly higher during reduced ASM compared with full ASM doses.
SIGNIFICANCE: EI maps are not uniformly stable across seizures. ASM reduction may broaden or intensify EI-defined epileptogenic involvement, suggesting that ASM status should be considered when interpreting EI during SEEG evaluation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation to determine their clinical utility for surgical planning.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: The Epileptogenic Index (EI) measures the involvement of a recorded brain area during a specific seizure. This study shows that EI patterns can vary significantly between different seizures in the same patient. While sleep states do not change these patterns, reducing a patient's anti-seizure medications increases EI values, making seizures appear to spread more broadly. These medication-induced changes must be carefully considered to accurately map the epileptic network for surgical decisions.

papers.title: Etiology-specific spectrum of epilepsy syndromes (ESSES): Widening the concept of etiology-specific epilepsies-Report from the ILAE 2021-2025 Terminology Commission.
papers.title_zh: 癫痫综合征的病因特异性谱系（ ESSES ） ：拓宽病因特异性癫痫的概念-来自ILAE 2021-2025术语委员会的报告。
papers.abstract: A new type of epilepsy syndrome, an etiology-specific epilepsy syndrome, was defined in 2022 in recognition of major advances in identifying the many genetic and acquired etiologies underlying the epilepsies. An etiology-specific epilepsy syndrome refers to where a known etiology is associated with a distinctive epilepsy presentation, including age at seizure onset, seizure types, and other morbidities, such as learning difficulties or intellectual disability, psychiatric features, gut and musculoskeletal problems. However, as we understand more about a specific etiology, such as a gene, it is clear that many etiologies are associated not just with one epilepsy syndrome, but with a range of epilepsy syndromes. Different epilepsy syndromes due to an abnormality in the same gene may reflect different types of dysfunction caused by the specific pathogenic genetic variant. Here, we expand the concept because-knowing the genetic etiology is not enough to ensure optimal clinical care-it requires a more nuanced approach to ensure the patient is managed appropriately. We define the concept of an etiology-specific spectrum of epilepsy syndromes (ESSES), which incorporates understanding the range of epilepsy syndromes that may be associated with a specific etiology. In some cases, a genetic etiology may be associated with a functional spectrum, such as pathogenic variants in an ion channel subunit that cause loss-of-function, gain-of-function, or mixed functional effects, each associated with specific epilepsy syndromes that may require different treatment approaches. With other genes, the functional effect may not yet be known, but their spectrum of epilepsy syndromes may be well established through genotype-phenotype studies. The concept of ESSES has the flexibility to grow in its scope with new insights gained from understanding the breadth of epilepsy syndromes associated with a specific etiology and the associated functional impact.

papers.title: Knowledge, self-management, and health-related quality of life among Omani adults with generalized epilepsy: A cross-sectional study.
papers.title_zh: 阿曼全身性癫痫患者的知识、自我管理和健康相关生活质量：一项横断面研究。
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: To assess epilepsy-related knowledge, self-management (SM) practices, and health-related quality of life (HR-QoL) among Omani adults with generalized epilepsy and to examine the correlations between these variables.
METHODS: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 200 Omani adults with epilepsy attending three tertiary hospitals in Muscat. Knowledge was measured using the Epilepsy Knowledge Scale-19, SM practices using the Epilepsy Self-Management Scale, and HR-QoL using the Quality of Life in Epilepsy-31. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and inferential statistics with a significance level of p ≤ 0.05.
RESULTS: Slightly more than half of the participants were male (52.5%), with ages ranging from 18 to 75 years (M = 33.29). Overall, participants demonstrated poor knowledge (M = 7.81/19), acceptable SM skills (M = 131.60/190), and low HR-QoL (M = 56.55/100). A significant positive correlation was found between knowledge and HR-QoL (r = 0.261, p < 0.001), whereas the correlations between knowledge and SM skills and between SM practices and HR-QoL were not significant (p = 0.710 and p = 0.104, respectively). Female gender, unemployment, presence of comorbidities, older age (≥ 50 years), and more frequent recent seizures were all significantly associated with lower HR-QoL (p ≤ 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Omani adults with epilepsy exhibit poor knowledge, only acceptable self-management skills, and low HR-QoL. The positive association between knowledge and HR-QoL highlights the need to strengthen epilepsy-related education. Culturally tailored educational and self-management support for patients, families, and the wider public is required to improve knowledge, optimize self-management, and enhance HR-QoL in Oman.

papers.title: Cannabidiol in pediatric drug-resistant epilepsies: A systematic review and meta-analysis of seizure responder rates and neurobehavioral outcome reporting.
papers.title_zh: 小儿耐药性癫痫中的大麻二酚：癫痫反应率和神经行为结局报告的系统综述和荟萃分析。
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as an important adjunctive treatment option for pediatric drug-resistant epilepsies (DREs), particularly in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) such as Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. However, the current literature remains heterogeneous and predominantly focused on seizure outcomes, with limited evaluation of broader neurodevelopmental domains.
METHODS: A systematic review with meta-analysis of proportions was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for studies evaluating CBD treatment in pediatric epilepsies (search updated to October 1st 2026), supplemented by citation searching. Randomized controlled trials and observational studies were included; secondary reports of the same cohort (extensions, post hoc and sub-analyses) were linked to their parent study. Extracted variables included study design, epilepsy syndrome, follow-up duration, seizure outcomes, cognitive outcomes, and behavioral outcomes. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients achieving ≥ 50% seizure reduction at the earliest stable post-titration timepoint, pooled across all studies with ≥ 10 assessed patients using a random-effects model (logit transformation, DerSimonian-Laird estimator).
RESULTS: Sixty-three studies (92 reports) were included, predominantly observational (56/63, 88.9%). The meta-analysis included 37 studies (3439 assessed patients; 1610 responders) and yielded a pooled ≥ 50% responder rate of 48.4% (95% CI 44.5-52.3), with substantial heterogeneity (I²=76.4%; 95% prediction interval 29.4-67.8%). Responder rates were lower in the CBD arms of randomized trials (41.3%) than in observational studies (49.8%), and higher at long-term than at short-term assessments (57.4% vs 42.8%). Seizure outcomes were reported in 98.4% of included studies, whereas cognitive and behavioral outcomes were reported in only 7.9% and 27.0% of studies, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Approximately half of children with drug-resistant epilepsies treated with adjunctive cannabidiol achieve a ≥ 50% seizure reduction in the available, predominantly observational literature; randomized trials suggest a somewhat lower proportion, and long-term estimates are likely inflated by selective retention. The literature remains strongly seizure-centered, while cognitive and behavioral outcomes are inconsistently assessed and poorly standardized. Future pediatric CBD studies should incorporate harmonized longitudinal follow-up and standardized neurodevelopmental outcome measures alongside seizure outcomes.

papers.title: Addressing stigma in epilepsy care: a systematic review of personalized anti-stigma interventions.
papers.title_zh: 解决癫痫护理中的耻辱感：个性化反耻辱感干预措施的系统综述。
papers.abstract: Epilepsy-related stigma (ERS) continues to be a significant challenge affecting people with epilepsy (PWE) worldwide and is closely associated with reduced quality of life and poor treatment adherence. Although various anti-ERS interventions have been developed, the effectiveness of personalized approaches has not been systematically evaluated. This systematic review synthesizes the available evidence on personalized anti-ERS interventions in epilepsy, focusing on their effectiveness as a strategy to reduce ERS. We systematically searched for studies evaluating personalized interventions aimed at ERS, including internalized, perceived, enacted, and courtesy stigma, and examined their effects on related psychosocial outcomes. We coded interventions across four personalization domains: age, culture, clinical/condition-specific factors, and setting. Of the 1,454 records screened, 74 studies from 34 countries were included, comprising 45 studies that directly evaluated the effectiveness of personalized anti-ERS interventions and 29 that indirectly assessed their potential impact on ERS through related psychological or quality of life outcomes. Overall, 78.4% (58/74) of interventions reported favorable outcomes, with favorable outcomes reported for 94.3% (33/35) of highly personalized interventions, compared with 73.1% (19/26) of moderately personalized and 46.2% (6/13) of low/basic personalization interventions. Few interventions targeted adolescents and transitional-age youth, and most studies were conducted in high-income countries. This study suggests an association between greater personalization and more favorable intervention outcomes. Personalized, collaboratively developed, culturally relevant, and developmentally tailored strategies are needed, particularly for adolescents and in low- and middle-income countries, alongside future research integrating standardized outcomes, long-term follow-up, and structural approaches to achieve sustainable stigma reduction.

papers.title: Impact of entry trajectory angle-to-skull on electrode placement accuracy in robot-assisted stereoelectroencephalography.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Despite the widespread use of robotic systems to improve stereotactic accuracy in stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG), targeting errors still occur. Several studies have suggested that the trajectory-to-skull angle is closely associated with targeting error among various influencing factors; however, quantitative analyses remain limited. Therefore, this study aimed to quantitatively evaluate the relationship between trajectory-to-skull angle and implantation accuracy and to establish practical cut-off values for surgical planning.
METHODS: A total of 10 patients (103 electrodes) were included in this study and various clinical variables were analyzed to identify whether trajectory-to-skull angle has a significant relation with accuracy using multivariate linear regression. Then, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis with Youden index optimization was applied to determine angle thresholds for achieving ≤ 3 mm accuracy.
RESULTS: Multivariate analysis showed that both axial and coronal trajectory-to-skull angles were significantly associated with target error, with more tangential incidence angles corresponding to larger deviations (p < 0.01). Axial angle-to-skull was particularly associated with anteroposterior (Y-axis) error, whereas coronal angle-to-skull primarily predicted superoinferior (Z-axis) error. ROC curve analysis identified optimal angle thresholds of 11.8° for axial trajectories and 6.3° for coronal trajectories to predict targeting accuracy within 3 mm. When both axial and coronal angles were maintained within these cut-offs, the probability of achieving a target error ≤ 3 mm was 88.2%.
CONCLUSION: Trajectory-to-skull angle is a key geometric determinant of electrode placement accuracy in robot-assisted SEEG. Quantitative angle thresholds identified in this study provide practical guidance for trajectory planning and may help minimize mechanical deviation, improve implantation safety, and enhance the reliability of seizure-network localization.

papers.title: DHDDS variants in epilepsy and movement disorders: Two novel mutations and an updated literature review.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Recent evidence suggests that dehydrodolichol diphosphate synthase (DHDDS, MIM*608,172) gene variation can cause neurological diseases. However, the complete clinical and genetic spectrum of DHDDS-related disorders has not been fully elucidated. This study aims to systematically describe the clinical and genetic features of five patients with molecularly confirmed DHDDS variants and to provide an updated review of previously reported cases.
METHODS: We retrospectively enrolled patients with DHDDS gene variants in the Epilepsy Center of Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University from 2021 to 2023. Clinical, neuroimaging, electrophysiological and genetic data were collected. Whole‑exome sequencing and Sanger validation were performed for variant identification and ACMG‑based classification. PubMed was searched using the term "DHDDS" to identify previously reported cases. The clinical and genetic characteristics of the eligible cases were summarized descriptively.
RESULTS: Five patients in our hospital with two novel DHDDS variants (c.623G>A, p.G208E and c.697C>A, p.P233T) were reported. A total of 74 patients (3 from our center and 71 from the literature) carrying pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were collected for the final analysis. The most prevalent variants were c.632G>A (p.R211Q, n = 26, 35.14%), c.110G>A (p.R37H, n = 16, 21.62%), c.109C>T (p.R37C, n = 9, 12.16%), and c.614G>A (p.R205Q, n = 9). The most common clinical manifestations included epilepsy (n = 64, 86.49%), intellectual disability (n = 62, 83.78%), ataxia (n = 50, 67.57%), global developmental delay (n = 50, 67.57%), tremor (n = 48, 64.86%), and myoclonus (n = 44, 59.46%). No significant phenotypic differences were observed among patients carrying different variants.
CONCLUSION: This study expanded the phenotypic spectrum of diseases related to DHDDS and reported two new variations. For cases of developmental epileptic encephalopathy of unknown cause, progressive myoclonus or complex movement disorders, DHDDS gene screening should be considered.

papers.title: Expert consensus on the clinical and organizational use of VNS therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy in the United Arab Emirates: a single-round modified Delphi study.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Epilepsy affects over 50 million people worldwide, and approximately one third of patients develop drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), a major driver of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) is an established neuromodulatory treatment option for DRE, but local guidance on its use in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) remains limited. This study aimed to establish an expert consensus to define best practices for the effective and efficient use of the VNS in the UAE setting.
METHODS: A multidisciplinary Task Force conducted a literature review and developed 25 evidence- and experience-informed statements, which were refined during an in-person expert meeting to ensure clinical relevance for the UAE context. Statements were rated through a single-round modified Delphi process involving UAE neurologists and neurosurgeons. Participants rated their agreement with each statement using a 7-point Likert scale. Consensus was predefined as ≥ 70% agreement, corresponding to ratings of 6-7. Statements with 60-69% agreement were classified as moderate agreement but were not considered to have reached consensus.
RESULTS: Fifty-six experts completed the Delphi round, corresponding to a 75.7% response rate. Item-level denominators varied across statements. Eighteen of 25 statements reached consensus, six demonstrated moderate agreement, and one did not reach consensus. Strong agreement was observed for patient selection, safety, structured parameter optimization, and multidisciplinary care pathways. Moderate agreement emerged for presurgical evaluation, timing of implantation, and selected clinical scenarios.
CONCLUSION: Building on existing international guidance and previous Delphi work in other settings, this study provides a UAE-specific description of expert agreement and variability on the clinical and organizational use of VNS for DRE. The findings may inform future local pathway development and identify areas requiring clearer definitions, prospective data collection, and further evidence generation.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This study asked expert clinicians in the United Arab Emirates to rate 25 statements on the clinical and organizational use of vagus nerve stimulation for drug-resistant epilepsy. Vagus nerve stimulation is an adjunctive treatment that aims to reduce seizure burden and improve patient-centred outcomes; it should not be interpreted primarily as a treatment intended to achieve complete seizure freedom. Eighteen statements reached the prespecified consensus threshold, while six showed moderate agreement and one did not reach consensus. Experts showed agreement on several areas, including multidisciplinary care, safety considerations, MRI compatibility, structured follow-up, and individualized programming. However, agreement was more limited for some topics, including expected responder rates after one year, timing of implantation, selected programming criteria, and quality-of-life effects independent of seizure reduction. These findings identify areas where expert views are aligned and areas where practice remains variable. They may support the development of more consistent local care pathways, while highlighting topics that require further clinical evidence and local guidance.

papers.title: Assessing cognitive compensatory strategy use in epilepsy: Pilot validation of the everyday compensation questionnaire.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Cognitive impairment is cited as one of the most consequential comorbidities of epilepsy. Cognitive difficulties may be managed using compensatory strategies. However, little is understood about how these strategies are used by adults with epilepsy. The Everyday Compensation (EComp) Questionnaire offers a means of assessing the use of these strategies but has only been validated for neurologically healthy older adults. The present study examined the preliminary psychometric properties of the EComp Questionnaire in epilepsy.
METHODS: 37 adults with focal epilepsy participating in a randomized controlled trial of a cognitive prehabilitation program completed the EComp Questionnaire, Quality of Life Epilepsy Inventory-31 (QOLIE-31), and the Instrumental Activities of Daily-Living Scale (IADL-C) at baseline and follow-up. Analyses included evaluation of internal consistency, construct validity, test-retest reliability, and item-level performance.
RESULTS: Across 20 imputed datasets, the EComp Questionnaire demonstrated acceptable Cronbach's α values. Test-retest ICCs were moderate (0.50-.58) but imprecise, with 95 % CIs spanning poor to good reliability. Correlations between the EComp Questionnaire and the IADL-C (ρ = 0.34, p = 0.04) and QOLIE-31 (r = -0.43, p = 0.007) suggested support for construct validity. Select items demonstrated low endorsement and weak association with the total score.
SIGNIFICANCE: Findings provide preliminary support for the EComp as a tool for assessing compensatory strategy use in adults with epilepsy. Understanding these adaptive behaviors and functional needs can assist providers in formulating treatment plans and interventions. Future research with larger and diverse epilepsy samples will be necessary to confirm structural validity.

papers.title: Parenting stress and life satisfaction among caregivers of children and adolescents with Epilepsy: A cross-sectional case-control study.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Childhood epilepsy imposes psychological burden not only on the affected child but also on caregivers. This study aimed to compare parenting stress and life satisfaction between parents of children and adolescents with epilepsy and parents of children and adolescents without a chronic condition, and to identify demographic and clinical factors associated with these outcomes among parents of children and adolescents with epilepsy.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 58 parents of children and adolescents aged 9-19 years with epilepsy and 44 parents of hospital-based control children and adolescents without a chronic condition (N = 102). Questionnaires were completed by the responding parent, typically whichever parent accompanied the child or adolescent to the clinical visit. Parenting stress and life satisfaction were assessed using the Parenting Stress Index-Short Form (PSI-SF) and the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), respectively. The SWLS captured the responding parent's own global life satisfaction. Group comparisons were performed using Welch's t test or the Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate. Multiple linear regression was used to identify factors independently associated with parenting stress and life satisfaction, with Holm-Bonferroni correction applied for multiple comparisons.
RESULTS: Parents in the epilepsy group reported higher PSI-SF total scores than controls (84.88 ± 24.04 vs. 72.73 ± 18.61, P = 0.005, Hedges' g = 0.55); among the subscales, the difference in Parental Distress remained significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, whereas the differences in Parent-Child Dysfunctional Interaction and Difficult Child did not. Life satisfaction did not differ significantly between groups (22.77 ± 7.00 vs. 23.98 ± 7.49, P = 0.442), and the confidence interval did not exclude a meaningful difference. Group membership remained associated with parenting stress after adjustment for the measured demographic covariates (child/adolescent age and sex, paternal education, and economic status) (b = 12.13, P = 0.010). Within the epilepsy group, parents of children with a seizure reported within the preceding 6 months had higher PSI-SF scores than parents of children without such a seizure (102.1 ± 22.0 vs. 81.1 ± 23.0, P = 0.027); all clinical analyses were exploratory.
CONCLUSION: In this hospital-based sample, parents of children and adolescents with epilepsy reported higher PSI-SF scores than parents of controls, whereas findings for life satisfaction and for seizure-related determinants were inconclusive or exploratory. Given the limited neurological phenotyping available in this sample, these findings primarily reflect elevated caregiver stress rather than identify specific clinical drivers of that stress. These findings support routine psychosocial screening of caregivers as part of comprehensive care for children and adolescents with epilepsy.

papers.title: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) in quality of epilepsy care: A systematic review.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The current lack of an unambiguous and widely applicable quality indicator for epilepsy care could hamper epilepsy care. The main aim of this systematic review is to study patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) instruments that evaluate the quality of epilepsy care and inventorize the main themes covered as well as the measurement properties of these instruments.
METHODS: The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (ID: CRD42025637902) and reporting followed the PRISMA reporting guidelines for systematic reviews. Electronic databases searches were conducted on PubMed, Embase and Web of Science. Articles published up to 2025 were considered. Dutch or English-language articles with a focus on the development and validation of PROMs to evaluate epilepsy care were included. Reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, protocols and translations were excluded. Covered themes and measuring properties (validity, external reliability, internal reliability and readability) were extracted. Risk of bias assessment was performed using 'Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health measurement instruments' (COSMIN) guidelines.
RESULTS: The search resulted in 1,904 articles. Seven articles met our inclusion criteria, evaluating a total of seven instruments. Recurring themes included seizure control (n = 5), treatment (n = 5), daily life (n = 3), psychosocial functioning (n = 3). Less frequently addressed themes included diagnostics (n = 2), quality of life (n = 2), injury (n = 2), reproductive health (n = 1), sleep (n = 1) and informal caring (n = 1).
SIGNIFICANCE: Most instruments evaluating epilepsy care focus on seizure control and treatment aspects while other domains like daily activities and psychological functioning are less well covered. Including these domains is however advisable as they are important components of QoL.

papers.title: Neuropathological findings in 2068 individuals with drug-resistant epilepsy based on updated classification systems: A multicenter retrospective cohort study from China.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study was undertaken to investigate the histopathological spectrum of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in a large Chinese surgical cohort using updated World Health Organization (WHO) and International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) classifications, and to examine its associations with seizure onset age, lesion location, and postoperative seizure outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective, multicenter cohort study consecutively enrolled individuals who underwent resective epilepsy surgery between January 2011 and December 2020 at three Chinese hospitals. Histopathological diagnoses were updated by two independent neuropathologists based on the 2021 WHO and 2022 ILAE classifications, supplemented by immunohistochemistry and whole exome sequencing when indicated. Postoperative seizure outcome data were collected from medical records and telephone follow-up, with the primary outcome defined as Engel class I at 1, 2, and 5 years after surgery, and Engel class Ia assessed as a secondary outcome.
RESULTS: Of 2099 surgically treated individuals, 2068 with complete data were included. The predominant pathologies were hippocampal sclerosis (HS; 28.4%), epilepsy-related tumors (20.7%), and malformations of cortical development (MCD; 15.4%). Childhood onset epilepsy was associated with MCD and HS, whereas adult onset cases favored non-low-grade epilepsy-related tumors and vascular malformations, with developmental lesions presenting earliest. Whole exome sequencing confirmed mTOR pathway variants in 65.2% of focal cortical dysplasia II cases and SLC35A2 mutations in 62.5% of mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia and epilepsy cases. Among 293 individuals with complete 1-, 2-, and 5-year outcome data (284 included in the adjusted prognostic model), no-lesion cases had significantly lower odds of Engel class I at 5 years than HS (odds ratio [OR] = .21, 95% confidence interval [CI] = .08-.56, p = .002). Temporal lobe location predicted favorable Engel class I outcome (OR = 2.78, 95% CI = 1.31-5.90, p = .008). Engel class Ia results were not statistically significant.
SIGNIFICANCE: Applying the updated WHO and ILAE classifications in this Chinese surgical cohort helps to characterize the pathological spectrum of DRE and may assist in postoperative outcome evaluation.

papers.title: Migraine comorbidity in epilepsy subtypes: Association with focal versus generalized epilepsy and seizure control-A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Migraine and epilepsy are paroxysmal neurological disorders that frequently co-occur and share common pathophysiological mechanisms. Whether comorbid migraine is associated with epilepsy subtypes (focal vs. generalized) and with seizure control remains poorly understood. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate these associations. This study was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines. PubMed and Web of Science databases were searched from inception to April 1, 2026. Studies ascertaining migraine using the formal diagnostic criteria defined by the International Headache Society or a predefined migraine ascertainment method, including validated screening instruments or questionnaires, were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and studies scoring seven or higher were included in a random-effects meta-analysis. A total of 8250 records were identified; 15 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis and six in the quantitative synthesis. Migraine comorbidity was not significantly associated with epilepsy subtypes (odds ratio [OR] = 1.10, 95% confidence interval [CI] = .84-1.43; I 2  = 32.1%). The primary analysis showed no significant association between comorbid migraine and favorable seizure control status (OR = .70, 95% CI = .45-1.11; I 2  = 63.2%). However, a separate exploratory, hypothesis-generating sensitivity analysis yielded an exploratory association between comorbid migraine and less favorable seizure control outcomes (OR = .61, 95% CI = .41-.91; I 2  = 47.6%); all pooled estimates were based on unadjusted data. Current data did not show a significant difference in migraine comorbidity between focal and generalized epilepsy. Although the overall analysis found no significant link between comorbid migraine and favorable seizure outcomes, an exploratory, hypothesis-generating sensitivity analysis suggested a possible association with less favorable seizure control, warranting confirmation through prospective, syndrome-specific studies with standardized outcome measures.

papers.title: Atmospheric pressure, temperature, and online search activity for epilepsy: A daily time-series study.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Meteorological conditions have been investigated as potential short-term correlates of epileptic seizures, but findings remain inconsistent. This study examined whether daily meteorological variation was associated with population-level online information-seeking for epilepsy.
METHODS: A daily time-series study was conducted in Lombardy, Italy, from September 1, 2021, to September 2, 2026. The primary outcome was a reconstructed daily Google Trends series for the Topic Epilessia (epilepsy). Daily mean sea-level pressure and 2-m temperature derived from ERA5 were the primary exposures. Distributed lag nonlinear models evaluated cumulative associations over lags 0-7 days, adjusting for long-term and seasonal trends, day of week, and national holidays. Newey-West standard errors accounted for residual autocorrelation.
RESULTS: Among 1822 days with complete exposure histories, lower mean sea-level pressure (5th percentile, 1003.5 hPa) versus the median (1016.8 hPa) was associated with higher cumulative epilepsy-related search activity (difference, 8.98 units; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.66-16.31; p = 0.016). No clear associations were observed at higher pressure levels or at low or high temperature. The association remained evident in several prespecified sensitivity analyses, including a log-transformed outcome, but was attenuated in the positive-only analysis and was not replicated using the simple search term epilessia. Secondary analyses showed no clear associations for relative humidity or precipitation, but an inverse association with high wind speed was found.
CONCLUSIONS: Lower mean sea-level pressure was associated with increased population-level epilepsy-related Google search activity. The observed association corresponded to a 13.3-hPa reduction in atmospheric pressure, a difference commonly encountered during the passage of low-pressure weather systems. Although the direction of the association is broadly consistent with some studies reporting increased seizure occurrence during periods of lower atmospheric pressure, Google Trends reflects information-seeking behavior rather than clinical outcomes. Therefore, these findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as evidence that atmospheric pressure influences seizure occurrence.

papers.title: Neural mechanisms underlying loss of functional independence after stroke: EEG evidence of impaired motor-to-sensory directed connectivity on the affected side.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Post-stroke reorganization of the prefrontal-sensorimotor network is critical for functional recovery, yet single connectivity metrics fail to capture its multidimensional characteristics. This exploratory study investigates network reorganization patterns and their clinical relevance to motor function and daily independence using multimodal electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity analysis, including Coherence (COH), phase lag index (PLI), and Granger causality (GC).
METHODS: Resting-state EEG from stroke patients (n = 22) and healthy controls (n = 22) was analyzed. COH, PLI, and GC metrics were computed for key regional connections involving the prefrontal (PFC), motor (MC), sensory (SC), and parietal (PC) cortices and correlated with Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) and Modified Barthel Index(MBI) scores. For stroke patients, hemispheres were classified as ipsilesional (i, affected) and contralesional (c, unaffected) based on the lesion side.
RESULTS: Compared to healthy controls, stroke patients exhibited distinct reorganization patterns. Preliminary evidence suggests enhanced parietal-motor coherence (COH_cPC-cMC↑) in the unaffected hemisphere alongside reduced motor-to-prefrontal directed connectivity (GC_cMC→cPFC↓). Interhemispherically, the findings may indicate weakened information flow from the unaffected to affected motor/sensory areas (GC_cMC→iMC↓, GC_cMC→iSC↓), accompanied by reduced bilateral motor synchronization (PLI_iMC-cMC↓). Within the affected hemisphere, there was evidence of enhanced bidirectional parietal-motor phase transfer (PLI_iPC-iMC↑), whereas directed pathways were significantly impaired (GC_iMC→iSC↓, GC_iPC→iSC↓, GC_iPFC→iMC↓). Clinically, the affected motor-to-sensory pathway (GC_iMC→iSC) showed a strong negative correlation with the MBI (r = -0.61, P = 0.002), and both interhemispheric motor regulation (GC_cMC→iMC) and synchronization (PLI_iMC-cMC) were significantly correlated with functional deficits (P < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Post-stroke networks may exhibit a "local compensation-global impairment" reorganization pattern. The affected motor-sensory pathway (GC_iMC→iSC) may be a biomarker for functional independence and thus allow for guided sensory integration-based precision rehabilitation.

papers.title: Do neuroimaging data have higher-order interactions?
papers.abstract: Recent advances in the physics of complex systems have motivated the study of higher-order structure in neuroimaging data, including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and magnetoencephalography (MEG). Despite the proliferation of proposed measures, the meaning of "higher-order" is often left implicit, and the term is used inconsistently across studies. In this work, we clarify the distinction between higher-order interactions and higher-order dependencies. Higher-order interactions necessarily imply higher-order dependencies, but the converse does not hold: systems can exhibit higher-order dependencies in the absence of higher-order interactions, as in the case of Gaussian variables. We present several equivalent definitions of higher-order interactions for continuous data, illustrate them using simple model systems, and use them to assess the specificity of measures commonly applied in neuroimaging. We show that these measures are not specific to higher-order interactions. Consequently, although existing studies support the presence of higher-order dependencies in neuroimaging data, they do not provide conclusive evidence for the presence of higher-order interactions.

papers.title: Coarse motor-state structure across paired preoperative fMRI and intraoperative ECoG in patients with brain tumors.
papers.abstract: Presurgical motor mapping in patients with tumors near eloquent motor cortex is commonly based on task-evoked activation maps, yet local BOLD responses may be difficult to interpret in lesion-affected tissue because of anatomical distortion, altered vascular coupling, and variability in task performance. In this study, we used a four-state motor paradigm spanning Action, kinesthetic motor imagery (IMG), Watch, and recent-action recall (REC) - to test whether coarse task-state relationships are preserved across paired preoperative fMRI and intraoperative ECoG in10 patients with brain tumors. Activation summaries and preoperative task familiarization were used to support task engagement, representational similarity analysis (RSA) was used to characterize within-modality state geometry, and cross-modal RSA was used to assess shared organization. Across modalities, Action and IMG showed relatively similar response patterns, Watch was more distinct, and REC occupied an intermediate position that should be interpreted cautiously because of the fixed task order. Cross-modal RSA showed positive correspondence between fMRI and ECoG representational dissimilarity matrices, supporting a shared coarse state structure rather than fine-grained equivalence between modalities. These findings support a hypothesis-generating, relation-based complementary framework for interpreting functional organization in patients with brain tumors, while the limited state space, clinically determined ECoG coverage, fixed task order, and indirect verification of internally generated states warrant cautious interpretation.

papers.title: Transformer networks are robust learners of source localization for EEG measurements.
papers.abstract: EEG source localization is an ill-posed inverse problem complicated by measurement noise, electrode dropout from sensor miscalibration, and variability in the number of active sources. Classical methods such as eLORETA and LCMV beamforming impose regularization assumptions that degrade under realistic noise conditions and do not naturally extend to multi-source scenarios. Recent neural network approaches improve localization accuracy but are typically trained and evaluated under idealized conditions that limit their applicability to real-world EEG acquisition. This work aims to develop and evaluate a source localization model that generalizes across the noise levels, source counts, and electrode configurations encountered in clinical and experimental EEG settings.Approach: We present a transformer-based model for single- and multi-source EEG localization. Hundreds of thousands of simulated EEG measurements are generated from known source locations, spanning a range of noise levels, source counts, and electrode dropout configurations, to train and evaluate the model. We establish a systematic evaluation framework that explicitly factors in source region density, signal-to-noise ratio, and electrode availability, and benchmark the transformer against classical (eLORETA, LCMV beamforming) and deep learning baselines across these conditions. We additionally conduct a thorough ablation study on network architecture and training pipeline design.Main results: Across all tested conditions, the transformer consistently outperforms classical and deep learning approaches, with improvements as high as 12\,mm in mean localization error (MLE) for multi-source scenarios under high noise. Additionally, when number of sources is unknown, the transformer can correctly predict the number and location of sources and drastically out perform the threshold-based approach (e.g an F1 Score of 68\% vs 12\% when simulated at 25\% noise). The multiembedding transformers maintains reasonable performance under conditions such as electrode dropout and increased noise.Significance: By explicitly modeling the noise, electrode dropout, and multi-source variability that characterize real EEG acquisition, this work addresses a key gap between benchmark performance and experimental utility in EEG source localization. These results lay the groundwork for more robust localization techniques applicable to real EEG data, with potential relevance to applications such as brain-computer interfaces. The data and code for this work will be made publicly available to support further development and benchmarking in the field.

papers.title: Decoding attempted handwritten characters based on temporal endovascular neural features.
papers.abstract: We evaluated temporal neural features for motor decoding using a minimally-invasive endovascular brain-computer interfaces (BCI). We hypothesised that relatively long compound movements generate distinct patterns of neural activity that are encoded by temporal features.Approach. A single participant implanted with the Stentrode endovascular BCI attempted to hand write English characters, which were then classified offline and online based on the recorded brain activity. The input to the model was a one-dimensional trajectory of high-gamma power, summed across all channels to isolate the effect of temporal information on decoding performance.Main results. A small number of classes across multiple months was reliably decoded, showing that temporal decoding could identify stable patterns of brain activity associated with each handwriting movement. Across four online sessions, where each session contained 20-30 trials/character and 80-180 rest trials, the best performing (3-class) model achieved a mean rest recall of 87% as well as character recall and precision of 65% and 59%, respectively. These results showed that attempted handwriting can be used in an online multi-class selection BCI and that temporal neural features capture the internal user context. Linear warping of trials to minimise temporal variability, where all trials were modified to have the same duration, led to significantly increased decoding performance compared to classifying raw trials.Significance. The results from our participant showed that decoding brain activity based on the differences between feature trajectories across time can be an effective strategy for discriminating different movements. Therefore, BCIs may be able to use temporal information to reduce their spatial footprint, likely making them less invasive. Overall, our study shows that further investigation of temporal decoding across multiple participants and other recording modalities is warranted. Strategies for automatic temporal alignment are likely to further improve the performance of these systems.

papers.title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4-8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power.
APPROACH: Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0°) or troughs (180°), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components.
MAIN RESULTS: Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough-peak differences in total (4.6-7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0-7.8 Hz) power ∼50-440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen's dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin.
SIGNIFICANCE: To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing facilitatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

papers.title: Neuromodulatory interventions for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent an escalating global public health challenge with major socioeconomic consequences. Although anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies have introduced disease-modifying treatment options for early symptomatic AD, their benefits remain modest and must be balanced against cost, monitoring burden, and safety risks. Neuromodulatory interventions have therefore emerged as promising investigational strategies that may complement existing therapeutic approaches. This narrative review evaluates current clinical and neurophysiological evidence for seven major neuromodulation approaches: 40 Hz gamma rhythm sensory stimulation, also known as gamma entrainment using sensory stimulation (GENUS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), focused ultrasound (FUS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM). Integrating clinical findings with mechanistic evidence, we examine synaptic plasticity, neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance, oscillatory entrainment, and cholinergic signaling as candidate therapeutic mechanisms. A comparative matrix summarizes target specificity, invasiveness, stimulation parameters, and translational status. Finally, we discuss key barriers, including biological heterogeneity, protocol standardization, durability of benefit, caregiver burden, and the uncertain implications of continuous network stimulation for future personalized and closed-loop interventions.

papers.title: Digital health meets Parkinson's disease: a bibliometric exploration of wearable sensors research and emerging frontiers (2005-2026).
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Wearable and sensor-based monitoring technologies are increasingly used to support objective, longitudinal assessment in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, the global development, knowledge structure, and emerging research frontiers of this interdisciplinary field remain incompletely mapped.
METHODS: Bibliographic records on wearable and sensor-based monitoring technologies in PD were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus for the period from 1 January 2005 to 2 February 2026. Searches were conducted in title, abstract, and author keyword fields. Microsoft Excel, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and the bibliometrix R package were used to analyze publication trends, collaboration networks, co-citation patterns, keyword co-occurrence, clustering, citation bursts, historiographic patterns, and source impact.
RESULTS: A total of 3,332 publications were included. Publication output increased rapidly over the study period, particularly after 2019, while 2026 represented an incomplete publication year because the search was conducted on 2 February 2026. The United States (U.S.), China, and European countries constituted the main knowledge-production and collaboration structure. Thematic analyses suggested a gradual shift from engineering validation and objective motor-symptom quantification toward AI-enabled digital biomarkers, remote monitoring, multimodal monitoring, and closed-loop neuromodulation. These patterns reflect research activity and citation structures rather than direct evidence of clinical efficacy.
CONCLUSION: This bibliometric analysis provides science-mapping evidence on the evolution of wearable and sensor-based monitoring technologies in PD. Future work should prioritize standardization, multicenter real-world validation, clinical workflow integration, multimodal data fusion, and cautious evaluation of closed-loop applications.

papers.title: Effect of epidural spinal cord stimulation combined with personalized neurorehabilitation in chronic motor-complete spinal cord injury: study protocol for the phase II single-arm feasibility RESTORES (RESToration Of Rehabilitative function with Epidural spinal Stimulation) trial.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic motor-complete spinal cord injury (SCI) results in profound neurological disability with minimal prospects for functional recovery using conventional rehabilitation strategies. Emerging evidence suggests that epidural spinal cord stimulation (eSCS) can activate dormant spinal locomotor networks and restore volitional and autonomic functions when combined with intensive activity-based training. However, systematic evaluation of multimodal neuromodulation approaches integrating advanced rehabilitation and computational neurophysiology remains limited.
METHODS: The RESTORES trial (RESToration Of Rehabilitative function with Epidural spinal Stimulation) is a prospective, single-arm Phase II feasibility study enrolling 15 adults with chronic (≥1 year) motor-complete SCI (American Spinal Injury Association Impairment scale (AIS) A or B) between C5 and T12. Participants will undergo implantation of an epidural spinal cord stimulator followed by a 24-week program of structured stimulation-coupled personalised neurorehabilitation (five sessions per week). Clinical outcomes will be evaluated using standardized neurological and functional measures including the AIS motor score, Spinal Cord Independence Measure version III (SCIM-III), Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury II (WISCI-II), and Trunk Assessment Scale (TASS). Autonomic function and quality of life will also be assessed. Multimodal neurophysiological measurements-including surface electromyography (sEMG), electroencephalography (EEG), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and computer-vision-based movement analysis-will be performed to investigate neural recovery mechanisms and inform the development of adaptive neuromodulation systems.
STUDY OUTCOMES: The primary outcome is the safety of epidural spinal cord stimulation implantation, defined as the absence of device explantation for safety-related reasons within 6 months following implantation. Secondary outcomes include changes in AIS motor score, functional outcomes (SCIM, WISCI-II, TASS), autonomic function, quality of life, and neurophysiological biomarkers.
DISCUSSION: This study integrates neuromodulation, advanced rehabilitation technologies, and multimodal computational neurophysiology to evaluate both clinical efficacy and neural mechanisms of recovery following chronic SCI. Findings from the RESTORES trial will provide critical safety and feasibility data to inform future multicenter trials and the development of closed-loop spinal cord stimulation systems.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, Identifier NCT05644171.

papers.title: Case Report: An MDT-guided multimodal protocol for large-area stroke plateau - integrating neuromodulation with multimodal assessment.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This case report investigates the feasibility and potential value of an individualized precision rehabilitation protocol for large-area stroke, integrating multimodal neuromodulation under the guidance of a multidisciplinary team (MDT) and dynamic assessment.
METHODS: A 38-year-old male with right hemiplegia and global aphasia following large left hemispheric infarction underwent an 8-month MDT-managed program. A closed-loop "assess-decide-intervene-re-assess" framework was implemented, featuring periodic multimodal evaluations (clinical scales, DTI, fMRI, EEG, 3D gait analysis). The intervention dynamically combined conventional therapy with staged neuromodulation: repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) for aphasia and intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation (iTBS) for motor disorder, Brain-Computer Interface (BCI)-robotic training and task-oriented Virtual Reality (VR) for upper limb function, and biomechanical correction with custom insoles based on gait analysis.
RESULTS: Notable functional improvements were observed: LOTCA increased by 16 points, CRRCAE subscale improved by 60%-90%, FMA increased from 20 to 56, FMA-B reached 12, and MBI improved from 40 to 91. Neuroimaging revealed increased fractional anisotropy (FA) in the corpus callosum and right corticospinal tract, and elevated ALFF/ReHo in right frontal-temporal areas. Event-related desynchronization (ERD) decreased during BCI training, and gait parameters improved.
CONCLUSION: In this patient with large-area stroke who showed limited response to conventional rehabilitation, an MDT-guided, dynamically adjusted multimodal intervention was temporally associated with concurrent recovery across cognitive, language, motor, and daily living domains. The concomitant neural changes suggest possible trans-hemispheric network reorganization. These observations are hypothesis-generating and, while limited by the single-case design, provide a preliminary rationale for future investigations into precision neurorehabilitation approaches in similar complex cases.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ChiCTR2300069203.

papers.title: Brain-State-Resolved Consistency of Corticospinal Responses to TMS.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: An important feature of motor-evoked potential (MEP) responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the primary motor cortex (M1) is their substantial trial-to-trial variability. Ongoing brain activity at the time of TMS, such as the power and phase of the sensorimotor mu rhythm, influences MEP amplitude. It is unclear to what extent these endogenous brain states also shape the consistency of MEP amplitude across trials.
OBJECTIVES: We investigated trial-to-trial variability of MEP amplitude as a function of pre-stimulus mu dynamics.
METHODS: Twenty-nine healthy participants received 1200 single TMS pulses over the left M1 during simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) recording; 10 participants completed two sessions to assess inter-session reproducibility. Trials were stratified based on pre-stimulus mu power, phase, and interhemispheric M1-M1 functional connectivity. Brain-state-resolved MEP variability was quantified using the coefficient of variation (CV) within subsets of trials defined by similar pre-stimulus mu dynamics.
RESULTS: Trial subsets characterized by high mu power were associated with reduced MEP variability, indicating more consistent corticospinal output. In contrast, mu phase did not significantly influence MEP variability at the group level. Mu power group-level effects were reproducible across sessions in an exploratory test-retest analysis and across experimental sites.
CONCLUSIONS: We show that inter-trial consistency of MEP amplitude reflects a structured, brain-state-dependent feature of the sensorimotor network. These findings contribute to our mechanistic understanding of trial-to-trial variability in TMS-evoked responses. This may provide a basis for future TMS approaches aimed at reducing response variability and improving the consistency of neuromodulatory effects.

papers.title: NeuroTest: a benchtop testbed for evaluating sensing-capable electrophysiology and neurostimulation systems.
papers.abstract: The development of increasingly complex implantable neuromodulation devices requires extensive benchtop validation and testing prior to in vivo implementation. Our goal is to enable this in vitro testing by creating a benchtop system that is accessible, easy-to-use, and functions reliably across academic and industry environments, reducing discordant results that arise from discordant approaches. Furthermore, such a system paves the way for standardizing benchtop characterization of future implantable systems by establishing a repeatable and comparable methodology for validating these devices and their capabilities. Approach. We describe the NeuroTest Board (NTB), a low-cost, open-source device that combines a low-noise current source waveform generator with a high-precision data acquisition system. We provide information on its architecture, operation, and performance as an initial benchmark of the potential capabilities of the system. Main results. We demonstrate the use of the NTB to assess electrophysiology systems in two separate applications. In one case, we assess a commonly used laboratory system (the RHD2132 headstage and Open Ephys data acquisition system), while the second case characterizes an investigational neuromodulation device in development for human use (the CorTec Brain InterChange). Following this initial sensing characterization, we explore stimulation-related artifacts that would hamper in vivo data collection. With the NTB, we develop and evaluate artifact mitigation strategies for each system, thus demonstrating an example application of this benchtop testbed. Significance. The ability to test neuromodulation devices against a common benchmark will enable faster development of novel therapeutics by increasing inter-institutional reliability and decreasing troubleshooting time.

papers.title: Engineering Bidirectional Neuromodulation: A Review of Neural Excitation and Inhibition Technologies.
papers.abstract: Neuromodulation provides a means to perturb neural activity for investigating nervous system function and treating neurological disorders. Advances in stimulation strategies, molecular tools, functional materials and neural interfaces have progressively expanded the precision and versatility of such interventions. Yet neural activity can require regulation in opposing directions across different cellular, circuit and pathological states, motivating bidirectional neuromodulation that can both enhance and suppress neural activity. In this review, we examine the mechanisms and technologies that enable such bidirectional control across electrical, optical, thermal, mechanical, magnetic and chemical modalities. We compare these approaches in terms of spatiotemporal performance, penetration depth, specificity and safety, and examine the materials, transduction strategies and device architectures used to implement bidirectional neural control. We further discuss the applications of bidirectional neuromodulation in neuroscience research and the treatment of neurological disorders. Finally, we discuss the technical challenges and future directions toward more precise, independent and integrated bidirectional control, including its extension to closed-loop adaptive regulation.

papers.title: Conductive hydrogel bioelectronics for chronic neuromodulation: From biomimetic design and bioactive interfaces to integrated neural platforms.
papers.abstract: In biomedical engineering, hydrogel bioelectronics brings together the interface between flexible electronic devices and biological systems, opening up a new way for chronic neural regulation. Here we focus on the recent progress in this field, from material design to system integration. The design of high-performance conductive hydrogels is an entry point. The multi-level structure engineering strategy, such as the introduction of carbon nanotubes or conductive polymers, can raise the conductivity and mechanical toughness together. When biomimetic adhesion molecules such as polydopamine or tannic acid are added, the hydrogel has the ability of wet tissue adhesion, and anti swelling and active anti-inflammatory functions are also embedded in the material system. As a result, the resulting neural interfaces are not only more durable in practical applications but also ensure excellent biocompatibility. Turning to applications. How does this kind of material promote the development of chronic neuromodulation technology? Peripheral nerve repair, brain computer interface, spinal cord injury, autonomic nervous system regulation can be seen in several scenes. The long-term and high-precision recording and regulation of neural signals is exactly the most important link in these applications. Hydrogel electronics does have its own uniqueness in this regard. However, there is still a long way to go between laboratory research and clinical transformation. How to ensure long-term stability? Can controllable degradation be achieved in practice? Will the signal fidelity drop with time? How to optimize wireless operation and system integration? Large scale manufacturing is an unavoidable reality test. These directions are probably the worthy areas for follow-up research. Looking forward, if the lines of intelligent response materials, closed-loop sensing and control, and advanced micro processing technology can be screwed together, hydrogel bioelectronics may truly move towards the next generation of personalized, dynamic and adaptive neural diagnosis and treatment platform.

papers.title: Case Report: Beyond chronicity: sustained multidimensional response to spinal cord stimulation three decades after traumatic spinal cord injury.
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is an established treatment for refractory neuropathic pain conditions, yet evidence for its effectiveness in spinal cord injury (SCI)-related neuropathic pain, particularly after decades of persistent symptoms, remains limited. It remains unclear whether unusually prolonged pain chronicity and established neurological deficits affect the potential for a meaningful response to neuromodulation.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report a 60-year-old man with chronic incomplete SCI, bilateral spastic paraparesis markedly more pronounced on the left, and severe chronic neuropathic pain following a gunshot-related spinal injury sustained in 1991. Retained metallic fragments were located at T12-L1; however, a formal neurological level of injury and AIS grade could not be reliably reconstructed because a complete contemporaneous ISNCSCI examination was unavailable. The longstanding bilateral lower-extremity pain phenotype was clinically consistent with below-level SCI neuropathic pain, although formal classification was limited by the absence of an ISNCSCI-defined neurological level. After more than three decades of persistent pain refractory to multimodal conservative treatment, permanent SCS was performed with two epidural leads positioned at T8-T9. Stimulation was predominantly DTM-based, supplemented by individualized tonic programming and later activation of closed-loop stimulation. Pain intensity decreased from 8/10 at baseline to 3/10 at 12 months and 2/10 at 24 months. This sustained response was accompanied by improvements in self-reported disability, neuropathic pain features, self-rated health, and psychological well-being, together with sustained discontinuation of pain-directed pharmacological therapy. No neurological deterioration or device-related complications occurred during the 24-month follow-up.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates that a clinically meaningful and sustained multidimensional response to SCS can occur despite more than three decades of SCI-related neuropathic pain and established neurological impairment. Given the limited and heterogeneous evidence for SCS in this population, interpret this finding as an individual clinical observation supporting further investigation of neuromodulation in patients with longstanding SCI-related neuropathic pain, rather than as generalizable evidence for patient selection.

papers.title: Elevated local field potential power characterizes choreic storms identified by deep brain stimulator event capture.
papers.abstract: Some patients with hyperkinetic movement disorders may present with a severe and prolonged state of uncontrolled chorea and/or ballism, termed 'choreic storm', causing distress and prompting intervention. These events may be more frequent and severe in patients with childhood-onset movement disorders. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) can be effective for medically refractory dyskinesias including chorea, and the availability of event-based local field potential (LFP) sensing in clinically available devices present an opportunity to better understand the underlying neurophysiology of these episodic phenomena. We analyzed clinical, electrophysiological, and corroborating video data from a patient with a  de novo CEP85L  mutation (NM_001042475.2, c.2381A>G, p.Y794C) presenting with chorea-predominant dyskinetic cerebral palsy, microcephaly, and intellectual disability. The patient underwent bilateral pallidal DBS for medically refractory symptoms and showed improvement in her baseline chorea. However, choreic storms continued multiple times per week, requiring frequent rescue medications and/or emergency medical intervention. These episodes were associated with autonomic features and variable triggers. Family-initiated LFP event recording supplemented by concurrent video facilitated side-by-side analysis of clinical episodes, revealing elevated LFP power in the theta to low gamma frequencies during choreic storms compared to baseline event recordings. Episode-associated increases in LFP power captured during choreic storms may represent a putative within-patient electrophysiological correlate of these severe episodic exacerbations. Although requiring confirmation and extension in larger series, these observations suggest that adaptive stimulation paradigms could be useful for patients experiencing choreic storms.
